title: Green Potatoes: Why They Turn Green and Why You Should Be Cautious

seo.title: Are Green Potatoes Safe to Eat?
seo.meta_description: The green color is chlorophyll, but it signals light exposure that can coincide with higher glycoalkaloids. Broadly green potatoes are best discarded.
seo.search_intent: Understand potato greening and glycoalkaloid risk.

excerpt: The green pigment itself is chlorophyll and is not toxic, but greening signals light exposure that can also increase natural potato glycoalkaloids such as α-solanine and α-chaconine.
content_html:
A potato turns green after exposure to light and production of chlorophyll. Chlorophyll is not the toxin. The concern is that the same conditions can also increase natural glycoalkaloids such as α-solanine and α-chaconine.

When greening is obvious or covers a broad area, discarding the potato is the safest choice.

Green color and glycoalkaloids are not identical

Both can rise with light exposure, but the shade of green does not tell you exactly how much solanine is present. Greening is a useful warning sign, not a chemical measurement.

Possible effects

High glycoalkaloid intake can cause nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain and diarrhea. EFSA found acute adverse effects beginning around 1 mg/kg body weight in available human evidence.

That equals roughly 60 mg for a 132-pound / 60-kg person and 80 mg for a 176-pound / 80-kg person. The concentration in any individual potato is too variable to convert that into a reliable number of ounces of green potato.

Where glycoalkaloids concentrate

Skin, sprouts, eyes and tissue just beneath the skin tend to contain more than the inner flesh. A potato that is both green and heavily sprouted has multiple reasons to be discarded.

Can you cut off a small green spot?

A very small superficial spot on an otherwise firm potato can be peeled away generously. If greening covers a large area or comes with sprouting, softness or bitterness, discard the whole potato.

Peeling and cooking

EFSA reports that peeling and cooking can reduce glycoalkaloids, but the reductions vary widely with the method and potato. No household cooking technique reliably guarantees that a heavily green potato becomes safe.

Bitter taste

High glycoalkaloid levels can produce bitterness or a burning sensation. If that occurs, stop eating the food.

Prevent greening

Store potatoes away from light in a cool, dry, ventilated place. An opaque bag or dark pantry is better than a bright kitchen counter.

Bottom line

The green color is chlorophyll, but it signals light exposure that can also raise glycoalkaloids. A broadly green potato is not worth trying to rescue; discard it.

Sources

Glycoalkaloid risk information comes from the European Food Safety Authority.

faq.question: Is the green part of a potato solanine?
faq.answer: No. The pigment is chlorophyll, but greening can occur alongside higher solanine and chaconine.

faq.question: Can I peel a green potato and eat it?
faq.answer: A tiny spot can be removed generously; a broadly green potato is better discarded.

faq.question: Does frying remove solanine?
faq.answer: Cooking can reduce glycoalkaloids, but not predictably enough to rescue a heavily green potato.
